The [Hypotenuse Calculator](/hypotenuse-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Hypotenuse of a right triangle from its two legs (Pythagoras). Enter your side a (one leg) and side b (the other leg) and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Find the hypotenuse of a right triangle — the longest side, opposite the right angle — from the two shorter sides. It uses Pythagoras' theorem: the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides. Builders use it to square up a corner (the 3-4-5 triangle), navigators use it for straight-line distances, and it is the same maths behind the distance formula in coordinate geometry. This guide explains how to use it, the formula it applies, and a worked example you can follow with your own numbers.

## How to use the Hypotenuse Calculator

Start by entering your side a (one leg), then entering your side b (the other leg). The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Enter the two shorter sides (the legs) of the right triangle.
2. Read the hypotenuse — the perimeter, area and angle are shown too.
3. Both sides must be above 0.

## Formula

c = √(a² + b²), where a and b are the two legs and c is the hypotenuse. For a = 3 and b = 4: c = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Hypotenuse Calculator](/hypotenuse-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. A right triangle with legs 3 and 4 has a hypotenuse of 5 — the classic 3-4-5 triangle. Its perimeter is 12 and its area is 6. Try the same figures in the [Hypotenuse Calculator](/hypotenuse-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## The 3-4-5 trick

A triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 is always right-angled, because 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5². Builders have used this for centuries: measure 3 units along one wall and 4 along the other, and the diagonal between the marks must be exactly 5 units for the corner to be square. Any multiple works too — 6-8-10, 9-12-15, and so on.

## Same maths, more dimensions

The hypotenuse formula is the distance formula in disguise: the distance between two points is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the differences in x and y. Add a third dimension and it extends again — the space diagonal of a box is √(a² + b² + c²). The same idea works in any number of dimensions.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- The hypotenuse is always the longest side of the triangle.
- The 3-4-5 triangle is a quick way to check a right angle in the real world.
- Enter the two legs — the side opposite the right angle is the answer.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the hypotenuse?

The longest side of a right triangle — the side opposite the right angle. For legs 3 and 4, the hypotenuse is 5. Try it with your own numbers in the [Hypotenuse Calculator](/hypotenuse-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### How do you calculate the hypotenuse?

Square both legs, add them, and take the square root: c = √(a² + b²). For 3 and 4: √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. Try it with your own numbers in the [Hypotenuse Calculator](/hypotenuse-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is the 3-4-5 triangle?

A right triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5. Because 3² + 4² = 5², it is always right-angled — builders use it to square up corners. Try it with your own numbers in the [Hypotenuse Calculator](/hypotenuse-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Can I find a leg if I know the hypotenuse?

Yes: a = √(c² − b²). Rearrange Pythagoras' theorem to solve for the missing side. Try it with your own numbers in the [Hypotenuse Calculator](/hypotenuse-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.
